chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazal, from Al-Hasan ibn Al-Jaham, who said:

I asked Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who died and had a debt upon me, and he left behind children: men, women, and young boys. So a man from among them came and said, 'You are free from what my father had upon you from my share, and you are free from what is for my brothers and sisters, and I am responsible for their pleasure regarding you.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'You will be at ease from that and free.' I said, 'But if he does not give them?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'That would be upon his neck.'

I said, 'But if the inheritors return to me and say, 'Give us our right'?'' He (peace be upon him) said: 'That is for them in the apparent judgment. As for between you and Allah (Exalted and Majestic), you are free from it, if the man who freed you takes responsibility for you regarding their pleasure, so the guarantor carries it for you.' I said, 'So what do you say about the child, for his mother to free (on his behalf)?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, if she has what satisfies him or gives him.' I said, 'But if she does not have anything?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Then no.' I said, 'I have heard you say that her freeing is permissible?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'I only mean that if she has wealth.'

I said, 'So is it permissible for the father to free (on behalf of) his son?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'For him is what was for us with Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him), a matter he does regarding that whatever he wishes.' I said, 'The man guaranteed to me regarding that child, and I am free from his share. So if the man dies before the child reaches adulthood, there is nothing upon him.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The matter is permissible according to what he stipulated for you.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a debt if one heir pays or guarantees it for the others?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia jurisprudence of 'tahlil' (exemption) in debt settlement, emphasizing the distinction between apparent legal rights (between people) and divine absolution (between the individual and God). It highlights the scholarly principle that a single heir’s guarantee, if accepted by the creditor, suffices for full release from the debt's spiritual burden, even if other heirs later dispute the distribution, provided the guarantor assumes liability. This ruling underscores the flexibility in commercial transactions within Shia law, prioritizing the creditor’s satisfaction and the guarantor’s commitment over rigid collective liability.
